nameStory: Lemon verbena gets its delightful name from the incredible citrusy fragrance that bursts forth when you crush its leaves between your fingers. The word 'verbena' comes from ancient Latin meaning 'sacred branch,' as many verbena family plants were considered sacred by Romans and used in religious ceremonies.
description: Lemon verbena is a tender perennial herb originally from South America that's grown in New England gardens for its intensely fragrant, lemon-scented leaves. This bushy plant typically reaches 3-6 feet tall with long, narrow leaves arranged in groups of three around the stem. While it produces small clusters of tiny white or pale purple flowers in summer, most gardeners treasure it primarily as a culinary and aromatic herb rather than for its modest blooms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly rough and papery, arranged in whorls of three around the stem. When crushed, they release an incredibly strong, sweet lemon scent that's unmistakable.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or very pale purple flowers clustered in delicate, airy spikes at branch tips during summer. Each individual flower is only about 1/8 inch across.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an upright, somewhat woody-stemmed bush that can get quite tall and wide. Stems are square in cross-section, typical of the verbena family.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are green and herbaceous, while older stems develop a light brown, slightly woody texture but remain relatively soft compared to true shrubs.

habitat: In New England, lemon verbena is exclusively found in cultivation - in herb gardens, container plantings, and sunny garden beds. It thrives in well-drained soil and full sun locations, often planted near patios or walkways where people can easily brush against it to release its fragrance. Since it's not cold-hardy in our climate, it's typically grown as an annual or brought indoors for winter.

seasonality.spring: Young plants appear in garden centers and are planted out after the last frost. New growth emerges with bright green, strongly scented leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush foliage and small flower clusters appearing at branch tips. This is when the fragrance is strongest and leaves are harvested for teas and cooking.
seasonality.fall: Plants may continue flowering until the first frost, but cold weather quickly damages the tender foliage, causing leaves to blacken and drop.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely outdoors in New England's climate. Some gardeners bring potted plants indoors where they may go dormant or continue growing weakly.

funFact: Lemon verbena leaves contain the same fragrant compound (citral) found in lemongrass and lemon balm, but in much higher concentrations - so high that a single leaf can perfume an entire cup of tea, and the scent will literally stick to your fingers for hours after touching the plant!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with lemon balm, but lemon verbena has much narrower, rougher leaves arranged in groups of three, while lemon balm has broader, softer, heart-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs. Lemon verbena's scent is also much more intensely citrusy and long-lasting.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'lemon verbena,' this plant is actually from a different genus (Aloysia) than the true verbenas (Verbena species) that grow wild in New England. The Spanish and Portuguese brought this aromatic treasure from South America to Europe in the 1600s, and it's been a beloved garden herb ever since.
compareHints: Lemon verbena is the only member of the Aloysia genus commonly grown in New England. Among other verbena family members in our region, it's easily distinguished by its intense lemon fragrance and tender, non-hardy nature - unlike our native wild verbenas which are hardy perennials with little to no scent and very different flower structures.
